title: State did not do critical risk assessment on Key Bridge before collapse, NTSB says
summary: The Maryland Transportation Authority never conducted a risk assessment on the Francis Scott Key Bridge that would have shown the 47-year-old span was well over the established risk threshold for collapse due to a vessel strike, the NTSB said.
content:
By Thomas Robertson

The Maryland Transportation Authority never conducted a risk assessment on the Francis Scott Key Bridge that would have shown the 47-year-old span was well over the established risk threshold for collapse due to a vessel strike, federal officials said Thursday.

The remarks by National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy came almost a year after a runaway container ship ran into the Key Bridge in the early morning hours of March 26, 2024, sending it tumbling into the Patapsco River in a matter of seconds.

Homendy said that not only had MDTA never run the assessment recommended by the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials on the Key Bridge, but that as of last October, it had not done so for the Chesapeak Bay Bridge.

“Had they ran the calculation on the Francis Scott Key Bridge, the MDTA would have been aware that the bridge was almost 30 times greater than the risk threshold AASHTO sets for critical, essential bridges — 30 times greater,” Homendy said.

“What’s frustrating is, not only did MDTA fail to conduct the vulnerability assessment on the Key Bridge, they did not provide, nor were they able to provide the NTSB with the data needed to conduct the assessment,” Homendy said in a Thursday news conference.

The NTSB said that as part of its investigation into the Key Bridge collapse over the past year, it has determined that 68 bridges across the country that were designed before the AASHTO standards came out — like the Key Bridge — have not performed risk assessments from a potential ship strike. It recommended that the 30 owners of those 68 bridges across 19 states perform the assessment to calculate the risk of collapse from a ship strike.

AASHTO first published its vulnerability assessment calculation for new bridges in 1991. It noted in 1991, and reiterated in 2009, that existing bridges should be assessed to calculate the risk that a ship could strike them and cause a collapse.

The Federal Highway Administration has required since 1994 that new bridges be designed to minimize the risk of collapse from a ship strike. The Key Bridge was opened in 1977.

Data the transportation authority could not provide the NTSB included the speed of vessels passing under the bridge, vessel loading characteristics, water depths, environmental conditions, bridge geometry and capacity of the bridge piers.

“We asked for that data — they didn’t have it. We had to develop that data ourselves,” Homendy said.

She said that, had the MDTA conducted the vulnerability assessment, it would have been able to take steps to reduce the risk of the collapse.

Six of the eight workers who were on the bridge when it collapsed after being struck by the cargo ship Dali, cutting off access to the Port of Baltimore and severing Interstate 695 over the river. Recovery crews were able to clear the channle and reopen the port in just a few months, but it will be years before a replacement bridge can be constructed to allow Baltimore Beltway and East Coast trucking to resume on I-695.

The NTSB is investigating all aspect of the crash and collapse, including what happened on the Dali, which lost power before it rammed into the bridge.
